items.text: AMEND AND RECOMMIT TO ENVIRONMENTAL CONSERVATION

items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the environmental conservation law, in relation to the central pine barrens area and the core preservation area
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S6157

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the environmental conservation law,
in relation to the central pine barrens area and the core preservation
area

 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL :

The purpose of the bill is to amend the boundaries of the central pine
barrens area and the core preservation area contained within,
established pursuant to ECL Article 57.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 amends subdivisions 10 and 11 of § 57-0107 of the
Environmental Conservation Law. Section 2 contains an effective date
and a severability clause.

 JUSTIFICATION :

This legislation expands the core preservation area of the central
pine barrens through the inclusion of two environmentally sensitive
areas located adjacent to the central pine barrens boundary - the
Shoreham property/Wading River Marsh complex and the Mastic Woods
complex. The Shoreham/Wading River complex consists of more than 800
acres of property containing extensive woodlands, fields, tidal marsh,
a vernal pool, and nearly one-mile of shorefront on Long Island Sound.
Based on inventory work by the New York Natural Heritage program this
property contains more than a dozen rare plant populations and is
composed of twenty-five distinct ecological communities. The Mastic
Woods complex contains several forested pine barrens communities,
providing habitat to many dozens of indigenous bird, mammal, and
reptile and amphibian species, including habitat for the federally
threatened Northern long-eared bat. It also encompasses the largest
remaining undeveloped property within the Forge River watershed. This
river is among the most significantly impaired waterbodies on Long
Island and preservation of the woodlands will help prevent further
deterioration.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

This is a new bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS :

None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect on the first of January next succeeding
enactment on which it shall have become a law.

items.memoText:
VETO MESSAGE - No. 245
 
TO THE SENATE:
 
I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bill:
 
Senate Bill Number 6157-B, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT to amend the environmental conservation law, in relation to
      the central pine barrens area and the core preservation area"
 
    NOT APPROVED
 
  This bill would add approximately 1,100 acres of privately owned  land
currently  zoned for industrial use to the Central Pine Barrens Area and
the Core Pine Barrens Area, effectively preventing  any  development  on
this acreage. Not coincidentally, this acreage appears to encompass land
owned  by  two private landowners who were in various stages of planning
and obtaining approvals for solar energy projects.  I  am  dedicated  to
preserving  the  Long Island's Pine Barrens and other open space on Long
Island. However, this bill, which passed without any public hearings  or
notice  to  the  landowners, is not the appropriate avenue to accomplish
that worthy goal. It unnecessarily pits land preservation against renew-
able energy, both of which are necessary to preserve the  State's  envi-
ronment  and natural resources for future generations, and both of which
have been foundational principles of my environmental and  energy  poli-
cies.
 
  I  am  committed  to  making New York State a national leader in clean
energy. New York's Clean Energy Standard mandates 50% of electricity  to
come  from  renewable  energy sources like wind and solar by 2030, to be
aggressively phased in over the next  several  years.  Renewable  energy
reduces  carbon  emissions, keeps the air clean, creates well-paid green
jobs, and improves the quality of life for generations  of  New  Yorkers
now and in the future. Siting renewable energy projects can be challeng-
ing.  But,  it  would  set a poor precedent to invoke laws meant for the
preservation  of  environmentally  sensitive  land  in  order  to  block
projects that should be addressed by local communities or through estab-
lished State siting or environmental review processes.
 
  My  administration  has  also  led  the nation in land acquisition and
aquifer protection. Since 2011, my administration has spent $124,114,335
million on land  acquisition,  accounting  for  over  140,000  acres  of
preserved  land statewide. For the first time in the State's history, we
established a local land acquisition grant program to  protect  drinking
water  sources,  funding  the  program  with $110 million from the Clean
Water Infrastructure Act of 2017. On Long Island,  we  have  taken  bold
action to protect the sole source aquifer, including a $5 million Nitro-
gen  Action Plan, a $6.5 million groundwater study, working with Suffolk
County on a $388 million sewering project on the Forge River, and we are
funding septic upgrades and replacement programs  that  will  total  $75
million  over  5  years. This should leave no doubt that protecting open
space and Long Island's aquifer is one of my highest priorities.
 
  Yet, achieving land preservation by legislatively changing the  status
of privately owned properties purchased in order to install solar energy
after  environmental  reviews  have  been  completed and local approvals
obtained sends the wrong message to renewable energy proponents  and  to
 
those  investing  in  clean  energy. Land preservation can co-exist with
solar, wind, and  other  renewable  power  sources.  To  sign  the  bill
as-drafted  would be a step in the wrong direction by moving away from a
clean energy future instead of leaning into it.
 
  Finally,  both  of  the affected land owners have vociferously opposed
this bill, threatening litigation for an unlawful  taking  without  just
compensation.  The  land  at issue is purportedly valued at roughly $100
million. While I take no position on the merits of such a lawsuit or the
value of the land, I also see no need to  risk  exposing  the  State  to
protracted  litigation  and  potential  liability when other options are
available.
 
  To be clear: alternative solutions are possible and my  Administration
proposed  them  to  the  Legislature  multiple  times. My Administration
attempted to negotiate an agreement for the  Legislature  to  amend  the
bill  in  the  2018  legislative  session  that would have satisfied the
affected land owners, the environmental community that opposed the bill,
the civic organizations that supported it, and the  bill  sponsors,  and
would  have also served to advance my own bold renewable energy goal. We
proposed taking tracts of land out of the bill, adding  land  elsewhere,
swapping  land  with  the private land owners and the local governments,
and other possible solutions.  Unfortunately,  a  negotiated  resolution
proved unworkable.
 
  I  remain  optimistic  that  a  solution  can be reached in the coming
months that will satisfy all involved. Accordingly, I  am  directing  my
administration  to  work  with  the  bill sponsors, and other interested
stakeholders, to formulate a plan to add a commensurate amount  of  land
to  the Central Pine Barrens Area and the Core Pine Barrens Area, and to
advance that plan in the 2018 budget. I am confident that if the  Legis-
lature  wants  to preserve land and open space on Long Island, it can be
done in a fiscally and legally responsible  manner.  In  this  instance,
however, I am compelled to veto this bill.
 
  The bill is disapproved.                    (signed) ANDREW M. CUOMO
 
                               __________
